solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Liberal authority combine

blocks.note: a pro is an expert, someone who speaks with authority
to fuse things is to combine them

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat local council forming an alliance with another body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' looks like the political party, but it is the definition in its lowercase sense of generous or lavish.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal can mean generous or plentiful, as in a liberal helping, and profuse means abundant or lavishly given.

clue.text: Transient leader of Right finished

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the next word is wanted

blocks.note: the first letter of Right
something finished is over

explanation.surface: A short-lived leader of the political right whose career is already done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transient' reads as an adjective describing the leader, but here it is a noun: a person who drifts from place to place.
explanation.definitionFit: A transient is a wanderer with no fixed home, and a rover is someone who roams about the same way.

clue.text: Preview of a setter's bollocks

indicators.note: slang for rubbish or nonsense, so the letters before it are a mess to be sorted out

blocks.note: the letters as printed, used as fodder

explanation.surface: A sneak peek at the crossword compiler's nonsense, with a self-deprecating swear word.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is': 'of a setter' is bollocks, meaning scrambled. Bollocks is crude British slang for rubbish or nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A foretaste is an early sample of something to come, which is exactly what a preview offers.

clue.text: Labour's reward: some colossal 'Aryan'?

indicators.note: taking only some of the words means a run of letters lifted from inside them

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Labour Party's prize is some huge racially pure figure, sounding like satire on a political scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' with a capital looks like the party, but it is work in general: the pay for work is a salary.
explanation.definitionFit: A salary is the regular payment an employee receives in return for the work they do.

clue.text: "One's taking very little time with head – bad"

blocks.note: 'One's' read as 'I am', shortened to I'M
M is the abbreviation for a minute
head is slang for oral sex

explanation.surface: A quoted confession of someone who takes almost no time over a bad act involving their head.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude reading of 'head' is the one needed: as slang it means oral sex, giving ORAL, which fits the clue's theme of naughtiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Immoral describes conduct that is wicked or wrong by ethical standards, which is one sense of bad.

clue.text: see 20ac.
(& 25dn,) Dismissed by Brenda, Gap amounts to "alien territory!"

blocks.note: a batsman who is dismissed is out
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the late Queen, whose cipher is ER
a gap is an empty interval or room between things

explanation.surface: Someone sacked by the monarch finds that the gap in their life is foreign ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' just places one piece beside the next. Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, and ER is her royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: Outer space is the realm beyond Earth, the home that science fiction gives to extraterrestrial beings, hence their territory.

clue.text: 20/6 fancies he is playing Hamlet (article inside)

indicators.note: actors playing a part present themselves differently, so these letters take another form
something inside sits within another piece, so one set of letters goes into the middle of the other

blocks.note: the play's title, used as letters
the definite article

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister imagines himself in the lead role of Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: '20/6' is PRIME MINISTER from the linked clues. 'playing Hamlet' sounds theatrical but just means rearranging the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A leader in charge is said to be at the helm, steering like a ship's captain; the clue says the premier believes he is in command.

clue.text: Cheeky note about recruiting ESP nuts could be party conference highlight

indicators.note: to recruit is to take new members on board, so extra letters are taken in
nuts means crazy, so the gathered letters are thrown into wild disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An impudent memo about bringing in psychic cranks might be the talking point of a party conference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ESP nuts' looks like a phrase for believers in telepathy, but 'nuts' is the anagram signal for all thirteen letters gathered together.
explanation.definitionFit: The keynote speech is the main address at a political conference, usually delivered by the leader as the event's centrepiece.

clue.text: see 23dn.
Play fast and loose with the truth to get elected, say, and end up like a Russian tyrant?

definitions.text: end up like a Russian tyrant?

blocks.clueFragment: Play fast and loose with the truth
blocks.note: to lie is to be careless with the truth
a politician who is elected is in
to say something is to state it

explanation.surface: A cynical recipe for political success: lie your way into office and finish as a dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition by example: Lenin's embalmed body has been on public display in Moscow since 1924.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead leader's body displayed publicly before burial is said to lie in state, as Lenin's famously still does in his mausoleum.

clue.text: "Britain getting there" trashed by last of forlorn community members

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked, so its letters lie in a jumble
the last of something is its final part, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: BR is an abbreviation for Britain
taken as written
the final letter of forlorn

explanation.surface: A political slogan about Britain making progress, mocked by a gloomy group.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase looks like a campaign slogan; only 'there' is scrambled, while 'Britain' is abbreviated and stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Brethren is the old plural of brother, used for fellow members of a religious community or fraternal society.

clue.text: Long, tiresome passage: 'the ultimate in Boris's belief system'

indicators.note: the ultimate thing is the final one, so only the closing letter is wanted

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
a creed is a set of beliefs

explanation.surface: A dig that Boris Johnson's philosophy amounts to nothing more than a dull rambling text.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase sounds like a sneer at Johnson's ideology, but it only supplies a final letter followed by a word for a faith.
explanation.definitionFit: A screed is a lengthy piece of writing or speech, typically tedious or ranting, which matches a long tiresome passage.

clue.text: Internally probe senators owning corporation

indicators.note: internally means on the inside, so the letters sit within the next words

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: An inquiry into senators who have shares in a big company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporation' looks like a business, but it is an old humorous British word for a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a large paunch is fat, and obese means very overweight, so having a big belly fits.

clue.text: Fight the two main party leaders at all times – be cunning!

indicators.note: leaders stand at the front, so the opening letters are taken

blocks.note: to box is to fight with fists
the two main UK parties are Conservative and Labour; their initials
ever means always

explanation.surface: Advice to take on both party bosses constantly while using guile.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain's two main parties are the Conservatives and Labour. The leaders are their initial letters, not real politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: To box clever is a British idiom for acting shrewdly to get an advantage, so it means being crafty or cunning.

clue.text: Taxed senior Tory leaders were sick

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so the initial letters are kept

blocks.note: the first letters of the two words
to retch is to heave as if vomiting

explanation.surface: Elderly Conservative chiefs who faced a tax rise felt ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taxed' looks like a reference to tax, but it means strained, as in a taxing task.
explanation.definitionFit: If resources or a person are taxed, they are pushed to their limits, which is what stretched also means.

clue.text: "Maker of cabinets", US president impounds a writer?

indicators.note: to impound is to lock something up, so one piece is shut away inside another

blocks.note: Jimmy Carter, US president 1977-81
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A president credited with forming governments seizes an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cabinets' with the political theme suggests government ministers, but here they are cupboards; Jimmy Carter was famously a peanut farmer, not a woodworker.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter works with wood, building furniture such as cupboards and cabinets, so a cabinet-maker is one kind.

clue.text: Boris and his year's school chums? Not much on top!

blocks.note: Eton College, the elite school Boris Johnson attended
a school's crop is the batch of pupils from one year

explanation.surface: A dig at Boris Johnson's old classmates as being rather empty-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is the English private school Johnson attended. 'Not much on top' looks like a jibe about brains, but it describes a very short haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: An Eton crop is a very short, boyish hairstyle fashionable for women in the 1920s, leaving little hair on the head.

clue.text: No longer cocky, that is, without introduction to sexual proficiency

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the first letter is used
without in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: ex means former
pert means saucy or cheeky
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is
the opening letter of sexual

explanation.surface: Someone humbled after realising they lack any real skill in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like lacking, but it means outside, so the abbreviation for that is surrounds the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Expertise is skill or know-how in a particular field, and proficiency is the same quality of being skilled.

clue.text: (& 6dn.) Boris needs to prepare to fire cabinet colleague

blocks.note: to make it ready
a member of the cabinet

explanation.surface: Johnson must get ready to sack one of his own cabinet members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to fire' reads as sacking, but it belongs with 'prepare': you prime a gun before firing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson was the UK's head of government at the time, so he serves as an example of the role.

clue.text: Digger's suit

blocks.note: first meaning: tools for digging, read as 'diggers' in the plural
second meaning: one of the four groups in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: The outfit an Australian (a digger) or a labourer wears.
explanation.walkthrough: A digger's suit sounds like a workman's clothes; read the possessive as a plural of digging tools, then as a card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Spades are both garden tools for turning soil and one of the four suits in a standard deck of playing cards.

clue.text: Show up suddenly with cannabis? Trendy

blocks.note: blow is slang for cannabis
something trendy is in

explanation.surface: Turning up unannounced carrying dope, as the fashionable thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Blow is British slang for cannabis (in American usage it more often means cocaine).
explanation.definitionFit: To blow in is an informal phrase meaning to arrive casually or unexpectedly, which fits showing up suddenly.

clue.text: (& 27ac./10ac.) Never had it so bad over here – wants to relocate

indicators.note: relocating moves things into new positions, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as printed, used as fodder

explanation.surface: A twist on Macmillan's boast 'never had it so good': life here is so grim people want to emigrate.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Macmillan, Conservative Prime Minister, said in 1957 that Britons had 'never had it so good'; the clue turns his slogan on its head.
explanation.definitionFit: If you have never had it so bad, conditions are at their lowest point, worse than at any previous time.

clue.text: Hacks love going after drugs and drink

indicators.note: coming after places one thing behind another in sequence

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, so more than one is Es
hacks are journalists, collectively the press
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Journalists depicted as chasing narcotics and booze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drink' suggests alcohol after the drugs, but it is the coffee; hacks are journalists, as in the Private Eye sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso is a strong black coffee made by forcing steam through ground beans, so it is a type of drink.

clue.text: see 7dn.
Costly rice proved to be soggy

indicators.note: something soggy has collapsed into mush, so the letters lose their shape and reform

blocks.note: the letters as printed, used as fodder

explanation.surface: An expensive rice dish turned out to be mushy, a complaint about a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a bad restaurant review; 'Costly' is the definition and the rest scrambles two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something overpriced is sold for more than it is worth, so it costs a lot, which is what costly means.

clue.text: see 23dn.
Peter sneakily holds back 20/6, to beat the opposition to it

definitions.text: to beat the opposition to it

indicators.note: acting sneakily means doing things in a devious, twisted way, so the letters are scrambled
going back means turning round, so the letters run the other way
to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
PM is the abbreviation for Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Peter Mandelson-style intrigue: a fixer secretly restraining the Prime Minister to stay ahead of rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: '20/6' points to PRIME MINISTER from the linked clues, abbreviated as PM before being turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To pre-empt is to act first so as to forestall someone else, getting in ahead of rivals.

clue.text: Pushed-aside American was rude at the dinner table, taking top off?

indicators.note: removing the top of something drops its first part, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: US is short for American

blocks.clueFragment: was rude at the dinner table
blocks.note: belching at a meal is bad manners

explanation.surface: A sidelined American guest behaved badly over a meal, perhaps undressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking top off' suggests undressing, but it means losing the first letter of the rude act.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone usurped has been displaced from their position by another who seized it, so they have been pushed aside.
